name: Papyrus sheets
note: Already abundant wherever there is trade access to Egypt (Rome's is the best-documented supply chain). Writing surface, not an invention; wherever you cannot reach it, an equivalent local writing surface is what you actually use.

name: Parchment sheets
note: Already produced from animal skin wherever livestock and tanning knowledge exist. Durable, reusable, erasable, expensive.

name: Wax tablets
note: Wooden tablets are given a recessed face filled with a thin layer of wax. Marks are made by scratching the wax with the pointed end of a stylus, and the flat end smooths the wax to erase them, or gentle heating melts it level again, so a tablet can be reused many times. It is cheap and reusable, but the marks are easily rubbed or scratched away, so it suits temporary notes and calculations, not permanent records.

name: Codex binding
note: Pages of papyrus or parchment are stacked and sewn together along the spine, then bound in a protective cover. This replaces the scroll, where text is written on a continuous roll that must be unrolled to find passages. The real advantage is fast access, as any page can be found directly without unwinding, speeding up reference and study.

name: Scribal copying
note: Scribes copy manuscripts by hand, one at a time, from an original text. This requires years of training to write quickly and accurately. Because every copy must be done by hand, texts are rare and expensive, and knowledge is controlled by the few who can read and the scribes who make copies available. This limits knowledge spread.

name: Carbon ink
note: Carbon ink is made by suspending lampblack (fine soot collected from burning oil or wood) or ground charcoal in a plant gum, which makes it flow and stick to the writing surface. It was used with brush and reed pen on papyrus and parchment. The carbon never fades, but it sits on the surface instead of soaking in, so it can be washed or scraped off.

name: Seals and stamps
note: A seal is a design carved in reverse into stone, metal or bone. When pressed into soft wax or clay it leaves a raised image that shows the document came from the holder of that seal. Each seal has its own design, so it verifies identity and makes forgery of contracts and orders harder.

name: Mosaic and fresco
note: Mosaic and fresco are two ways of making lasting images on walls and floors. A mosaic presses small coloured stone or glass pieces (tesserae) into mortar. A fresco is painted with pigment onto wet lime plaster, which then hardens chemically and locks the colour into the wall. Both need skilled artists, and each image is unique and cannot be copied or moved.

name: Sculpture
note: Carving stone or casting bronze into a lasting three-dimensional image of a person, god or event. A sculptor works from a model, removing stone with chisels or pouring metal into a mould. It needs a skilled artist, stone or bronze, and tools. Each work is a single piece and cannot be copied cheaply, so a message reaches only those who come to see it.

name: Theatre and pantomime
note: A live performance of a story by actors, with words, dance or mime, before an audience gathered in one place. It needs a stage, performers who have learned their parts and a crowd able to attend. It reaches many people at once and can teach or persuade, but it vanishes when the show ends and cannot be repeated exactly or sent to another city.

name: Woodblock carving
note: Cutting a picture or text in relief on a block of wood, leaving the lines raised, then inking the raised surface and pressing paper or cloth onto it. One carved block prints many copies. It needs close-grained wood, sharp carving tools, ink and paper. It is the first cheap reproducible image and breaks the scribe's monopoly, but each page needs a new block and a block wears out.

name: Relief printing
note: In relief printing the picture is the raised part of a carved block, with the background cut away. Ink is brushed onto the raised surface and paper or cloth is pressed against it, so the raised lines print and the cut-away parts stay blank. It needs a carved block, an ink that sticks to the block (carbon ink bound with oil), and an absorbent surface to take the ink.

name: Hand papermaking
annual_output_basis: One vat worked by the crew of three that hand papermaking has always had (vatman, coucher, layman) at the thirteen hours a kilogram the entry states: three times two thousand hours over thirteen is about half a tonne of paper a year. Declared plant size from the entry's own hours, conf C.
note: Making paper sheet by sheet: rag fibre is beaten into a pulp, mixed with water in a vat, and scooped up on a wire mesh frame (a mould) so that the water drains and a mat of fibre is left to be pressed and dried. It needs clean rags, water, a vat and moulds. It is slow, one sheet at a time, and the thickness varies from sheet to sheet.

name: Water-driven pulp stamper
note: Paper is made from rags broken down into a thin mush of loose fibres. A water wheel turns a shaft with projecting cams that lift heavy wooden hammers, which fall into troughs of soaked rags and pound them. The machine works without tiring, so it makes far more pulp, and more even pulp, than people beating rags by hand. That is what allows paper to be made in volume.

name: Surface sizing
note: Coating the surface of paper with a sizing of alum and gelatin so the fibres are sealed. Without it, paper is like blotting paper and ink soaks through and spreads. With it, the ink sits on the surface in a crisp line, which printing requires. It needs rag paper, alum (a mineral salt) and gelatin, made by boiling animal hides or bones. Too little size leaves ink bleeding; too much makes the sheet repel ink.

name: Wire mould and deckle
note: A papermaking mould is a wooden frame covered with a mesh of fine brass wire. The worker dips it into a vat of watery pulp and lifts it, so the water drains through the mesh and leaves a flat mat of fibres that becomes one sheet. A removable rim called the deckle keeps the pulp inside the frame and shapes the edge of the sheet. Evenly drawn wire gives sheets of even thickness, and the wire spacing leaves faint lines visible when the paper is held to the light.

name: Fourdrinier papermaking machine
note: A papermaking machine that makes a continuous sheet: watery pulp pours onto a moving endless belt of fine wire mesh, water drains through, and the damp web is pressed and dried on rollers. It needs steam power to drive the belt and rollers, and parts made to close tolerance so the web runs smoothly. It makes paper in enormous quantity and displaces hand workers, who may protest.

name: Wood pulp from timber
note: Paper pulp made from timber instead of rag. The wood is treated with heat and chemicals (alkali) that free its fibres. It is far cheaper than rag pulp because wood is plentiful, but wood contains lignin, a substance that yellows and makes paper brittle over time. It needs a large supply of timber, a pressure vessel or boiling vat, and alkali. Bleaching and washing the pulp are the hard steps.

name: Oil-based printing ink
note: Carbon in heated linseed oil. Sticks to metal type. Water-based ink beads off metal, non-obvious blocker.

name: Type punch
note: A letter cut in relief on the end of a hardened steel rod, in mirror image, used to strike an impression into a softer metal. The punch cutter files each letter by hand, so letters must be exact; once it is made, it can be struck again and again to give identical matrices. It needs hard steel, files, a hardening furnace and tolerance to a tenth of a millimetre.

name: Type matrix
note: A small block of soft brass into which a hardened punch has been struck, leaving a cavity that is the negative of a letter. It is the mould for casting type, so a single punch yields a matrix that can cast type indefinitely. It needs brass and a steel punch. The matrix must be struck square and to the right depth, or letters will not align.

name: Adjustable hand mould
note: An iron mould whose sides slide to fit letters of different widths, with a matrix fitted into the bottom. Molten metal is poured in and shaken to fill the matrix cavity, producing a piece of type (a sort). One caster can make thousands of identical sorts per day. It needs a matrix and fine metalwork, because the mould must be uniform so all the letters stand to the same height.

name: Type metal alloy
note: An alloy of lead and tin with antimony added, used to cast type. Lead and tin melt at low temperature, easy to pour. Antimony is the key ingredient: it expands slightly as the alloy cools, forcing the metal into every corner of the matrix, and it hardens the type so it survives many impressions. It needs lead, tin, antimony and a crucible fire. A wrong mix gives soft or brittle type.

name: Composing stick and galley
note: Compositors set metal sorts in stick, proof, transfer to galley. Allows rearrangement before lock-up.

name: Platen press
note: A press in which a flat bed holds the inked type and a flat plate (the platen) is screwed down on top of it, pressing the paper evenly against it. It needs oil-based ink, which clings to metal type, a screw made accurately, and level surfaces so the impression is even. This was Gutenberg's innovation, and it reproduces a page quickly. A worn screw or uneven bed leaves faint patches.

name: Cylinder press
note: Rotating cylinder instead of platen. Type moves under rolling pressure. Faster, smoother. Steam power essential.

name: Rotary press
note: Two cylinders, type wraps around curved plate. Continuous feed and output. Thousands of sheets per hour.

name: Stereotype plate
note: A stereotype is a one-piece metal copy of a whole page of set type. A mould of the page is made by pressing damp papier-mache into the type and drying it, and molten lead-based type metal is poured into the mould and cools into a solid plate. The pour has to be quick and even or the plate is flawed. The plate can be cast curved to wrap round a cylinder, which rotary presses need, and the original type is free to be reused at once.

name: Electrotype plate
note: Electroplated copper shell on lead backing. Sharper impression. More durable. Expensive.

name: Linotype machine
note: Operator taps keyboard, matrices drop, spacing added, hot metal poured into mould. Complete line emerges cast solid.

name: Monotype machine
note: A machine that sets and casts type one character at a time, controlled by a punched paper tape. A keyboard punches the tape, and the tape then drives a caster that makes each letter from molten type metal and arranges the letters into lines. It needs electric power, type metal and a precisely made casting mechanism. It is slower than the Linotype, which casts whole lines, but it offers flexible fonts and easy correction of single letters.

name: Intaglio engraving
note: Intaglio is the opposite of relief printing: the lines to be printed are cut as grooves into a polished copper plate with a hard steel tool. Ink is rubbed into the grooves and the flat surface wiped clean, then damp paper is forced into the grooves under heavy pressure and lifts the ink out. A groove can be cut very fine, so it gives much finer detail than carved wood blocks, but it needs a flat plate and a press strong enough to push the paper into the grooves.

name: Etching with acid
note: Making a printing plate by coating a copper plate with wax, drawing through the wax with a needle to expose the metal, then dipping the plate in acid, which bites only where the metal is bare. The plate is then inked and printed. It needs copper, wax, nitric acid and an engraver's skill. It gives fine tonal work without cutting by hand and is faster than engraving. The depth of bite depends on how long the plate stays in the acid.

name: Lithography
note: Lithography prints from a flat polished stone with nothing carved into it. The image is drawn on the stone with a greasy crayon or ink, and the stone is then treated so that the bare parts hold water. Greasy printing ink sticks only to the drawing and is repelled by the wet stone, so paper pressed onto the inked stone takes the image. The chemistry is not obvious, because the surface is sorted by grease and water and not by height.

name: Offset lithography
note: A printing method in which the inked image is transferred from the plate to a rubber-covered roller and then onto the paper, instead of straight from the plate. The soft rubber presses into rough paper to print fine detail, and the plate is never struck against the paper, so it lasts longer. It needs lithography and steam power for the presses. The balance of ink and water on the plate must be kept steady.

name: Halftone screening
note: THE invention making photographs printable. Cross-ruled screen photographed with image. Variable dots create tone illusion.

name: Four-colour separation
note: Printing full-colour pictures from four inks: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. The original is photographed through colour filters, giving a separate plate for each ink, and the plates are printed one over the other in registration (aligned exactly). It needs a halftone screen, which breaks tones into dots, filters, and careful plate alignment. If the plates are out of register the picture is blurred and fringed.

name: Newspaper institution
note: Daily publication breaks state monopoly on information. Political instrument. Cheap accurate copying enables rapid idea spread.

name: Typewriter
note: Keyed strike-through ribbon. QWERTY deliberately slows typist to prevent jams. Shift key accesses capitals.

name: Silver halide chemistry
note: Silver nitrate and sodium chloride form photosensitive silver chloride crystals. Darkens on exposure. Foundation of photography.

name: Daguerreotype plate
note: Polished copper plate, silver-coated, exposed to light, developed in mercury vapour. Mirror-like image. Cannot be copied.

name: Calotype negative-positive
note: A photographic process which makes a paper negative, from which any number of positive prints can be made. Paper is coated with silver salts, exposed in a camera, developed, and then used as a negative to print on other sensitised paper. The negative is the invention: one exposure yields unlimited prints. It is cheaper than the daguerreotype, which makes only one image, but the paper fibres blur the detail.

name: Wet collodion plate
note: A photographic plate made by coating a glass sheet with collodion (nitrocellulose dissolved in ether and alcohol) containing silver salts. It gives sharper detail than paper negatives. The plate must be exposed and developed while still wet, because the coating loses its sensitivity as it dries. Field photographers therefore carried darkroom tents and chemicals with them. It needs good glass, nitrocellulose and silver halide.

name: Gelatin dry plate
note: Silver halide in gelatin. Sensitive when dry. Long shelf life. Easy storage and transport. Portable photography practical.

name: Roll film on celluloid
note: Flexible base allows compact cameras. Light and durable. Enables hand-held shooting. Photography becomes casual.

name: Optical enlarger
note: An optical device that projects the image of a negative through a lens onto sensitised paper, so that a small negative is printed much larger. Moving the lens or paper changes the magnification. It needs roll film or plates, ground lenses and a lamp. Contact printing can only give prints the size of the negative, so enlargement frees the camera from being large and unlocks the full detail of a good negative.

name: Colour photography
note: Multi-layer emulsion sensitive to red, green, blue. Complex chemistry. Colour casts and fading persist. Natural colour possible.

name: Magic lantern projection
note: A projector that shines a candle or arc light through a painted glass slide and a lens onto a screen, giving a large bright image to a whole room. It needs ground and polished lenses, a bright light and hand-painted slides. It allows mass viewing, so a lecturer or showman can reach an audience. A weak light makes the image dim, and a hot lamp can crack a slide.

name: Intermittent film movement
note: Sprockets and claw mechanism pull film frame-by-frame. Each frame holds still, advances in darkness. THE invention of cinema.

name: Cinema shutter
note: A rotating disc with an opening that blocks the light while a film frame is pulled into place and lets it through when the frame is still. The viewer therefore sees each frame sharply, not a smear of movement. It needs intermittent film movement, meaning the film moves in jerks, and a shutter timed with it. It also controls flicker: if the dark period or the frame rate is wrong, the picture flickers unpleasantly.

name: Cinema projection
note: A projector that throws the images of film frames, one after the other, through a lens onto a screen so that they appear to move. A bright arc lamp is the light source, the shutter hides film movement, and the film is pulled through frame by frame. It needs a darkened theatre, because the image is faint against ambient light. Hot lamps can ignite early film, which burns readily.

name: Film studio and stage
note: A large stage, usually roofed with glass for daylight and with strong arc lighting, where actors repeat scenes for the camera. It is the place where raw film is made for later assembly. It needs sets, lights, a camera and actors, and a director to say what is wanted. Early film is so slow that a lot of light is required, so a studio is an expensive building that must be planned around light.

name: Nitrate film storage safety
note: Nitrocellulose base extremely flammable and self-oxidising. Fires spontaneous and unstoppable. Underground vaults needed.

name: Phonograph with cylinder
note: A machine that records sound by having sound waves vibrate a diaphragm attached to a needle, which cuts a groove in a rotating wax-coated cylinder. To play it back, the needle runs along the groove and moves the diaphragm, which makes sound. It needs a steady motor, a precisely cut screw to move the needle along, and wax. The sound is thin and quiet, and the wax wears out after a few plays.

name: Disc record and lateral recording
note: Groove meanders side-to-side encoding amplitude. Shellac pressing from master. Playable from multiple copies.

name: Loudspeaker
note: A device that turns an electric signal back into sound: a coil attached to a cone sits in a magnetic field, and current in the coil makes the cone move to and fro, pushing the air. It works like a microphone in reverse. It needs an electromagnet or magnet, fine wire and a light diaphragm. The signal from a microphone is weak, so it must be amplified to be heard at a useful volume.

name: Electrical recording and amplification
note: Recording sound through electric means: a microphone turns sound into a signal, a valve amplifier (a vacuum tube circuit) strengthens it, and that drives a cutting stylus that cuts the groove in a disc. It captures bass and treble that purely mechanical recording misses, so fidelity jumps. It needs the disc record, amplifier tubes and a microphone. Poor amplifier design distorts the recorded sound.

name: Magnetic wire and tape recording
note: Steel wire or tape magnetised by recording head. Erasable and reusable. Linear response superior to disc.

name: Radio broadcasting as medium
note: Sending sound live from a transmitter to many receivers at once, so that anyone with a set can listen. It needs a radio transmitter, receivers sold or built in volume, and a programme to carry. Radio ignores geography, since a signal passes mountains and frontiers, so states take a strong interest in controlling who may broadcast. The costs of programmes must be met, often by the state or advertising.

name: Library and archive
note: A library is a building where texts are kept so that they outlive any one owner, and an archive keeps records. It needs shelves, a roof against fire and damp, guards against theft and literate people to look after it. It lets knowledge be shared between people and over generations. Fire is the greatest danger: Alexandria is the warning. Without a catalogue, though, a large collection is hard to use.

name: Cataloguing and classification
note: Ordering a collection by subject, author and title, recorded in a catalogue (a list of cards or entries) so that a particular work can be found without searching the shelves. It needs a collection, literate cataloguers and a consistent scheme. A pile of scrolls becomes a searchable resource. The hard part is staying consistent as the collection grows, because a scheme that is changed midway leaves two systems.

name: Index and concordance
note: A complete alphabetical list of the words in a text with the place each occurs, which allows a reader to look up any word or idea and find every passage on it. It needs a fixed text, patient literate clerks, and a way of locating a place, such as numbered pages or lines. It turns a corpus into a reference work. Compiling one by hand is very slow, and every revision of the text invalidates it.

name: Copyright and publishing economics
note: A legal monopoly granted to an author or publisher over the right to copy a work, so that they earn income from sales. It barely makes sense before printing, since hand copying a scroll is so slow that unauthorised copies are little threat. Printing makes copying cheap, so a pirate can undersell the publisher. It needs courts and a government willing to enforce it, and movable type.
